summary: Defines a data structure, a flow specification, that hosts can use to describe the quality of communication they need from the network, such as bandwidth. It was written for multimedia applications and published by the IRTF as an informational proposal.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1363 proposes a set of fields that lets a host describe the network service a data flow needs. The fields cover traffic amount, delay, loss and the strength of any requested service guarantee.

questions: network quality of service flow spec
how does quality of service work
subtitle: A proposed set of parameters for describing the service a network flow needs.

tldr.problem: Applications may need to tell a network how much traffic they will send and how sensitive it is to delay, variation and loss.
tldr.mechanism: The proposed flow specification uses fields for traffic rates, packet size, delay and loss sensitivity, and the requested quality of guarantee.
tldr.outcome: This Informational proposal offers a flexible description for experimentation; it does not define the protocol that negotiates or establishes a flow.

today: RFC 1363 is an Informational proposal published in September 1992, and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo presents the flow spec for information and possible experimentation, not as an Internet standard.

sections.title: Purpose of a Flow Specification
sections.content:
A flow specification, or flow spec, is a data structure that a host can use to request special handling for one direction of a flow. An application might need to describe requirements for bandwidth, delay or packet loss so the network can consider them when handling its traffic.

The memo defines the fields and their meaning, but does not define how hosts and networks negotiate a flow. It is an Informational proposal from the Internet Research Task Force, intended for information and possible experimentation by consenting routers and applications.
sections.plainLanguage: A flow spec lets a host describe what its data flow needs from the network. This memo defines the description, not the process that accepts or rejects a request.

sections.title: What the Fields Describe
sections.content:
The flow spec describes four kinds of requirements. It characterizes the traffic's sustainable rate, peak rate and burst size; indicates how sensitive the application is to delay; describes sensitivity to packet loss and consecutive losses; and states the quality of guarantee requested.

The delay-sensitivity field tells the network when further delay improvement is no longer useful; it is not a maximum acceptable delay. The delay-variation field describes how much variation the receiving host can accommodate, including through buffering. A separate field gives the maximum transmission unit (MTU), the largest packet in the flow.
sections.plainLanguage: The fields tell the network how much data to expect and how the application responds to delay and loss. They also state whether the host asks for no guarantee, predicted service or a firmer guarantee.

sections.title: Format of the Flow Specification
sections.content:
The format diagram contains fields for Version, Maximum Transmission Unit, Token Bucket Rate, Token Bucket Size, Maximum Transmission Rate, Minimum Delay Noticed, Maximum Delay Variation, Loss Sensitivity, Burst Loss Sensitivity, Loss Interval and Quality of Guarantee. Each field occupies 16 bits in the diagram. Version 1 is the version defined by this memo.

Most fields use a common encoding for numeric values or well-defined constants. The version and MTU fields use their own formats. A flow spec describes one direction; a flow that sends in both directions needs a specification for each direction.
sections.plainLanguage: The flow spec has fields for traffic size and rate, delay, loss and the requested guarantee. It describes one direction, so traffic in both directions needs two flow specs.

sections.title: Traffic Rates and Burst Control
sections.content:
The Token Bucket Rate describes how quickly byte credits build up, and the Token Bucket Size limits how many credits can be saved. To send a packet, a host uses credits equal to the packet size; if it lacks enough credits, it waits. This model describes a traffic pattern, but hosts may use any traffic-management method that behaves equivalently.

The Maximum Transmission Rate limits how quickly successive packets can enter the network. The memo describes this as a separate control from the sustainable rate and burst size. If the token-bucket rate is zero, the application is not requesting a bandwidth guarantee, and the token-bucket size must also be zero.
sections.plainLanguage: The rate and bucket size describe the flow's normal pace and the size of a burst it can send. A separate rate limits how quickly packets can follow one another.

sections.title: Guarantees, Use and Limitations
sections.content:
The Quality of Guarantee field distinguishes no guarantee, an imperfect guarantee, predicted service and guaranteed service, including whether an imperfect result is acceptable. The memo expects a network to accept or reject a request for a guaranteed flow. It also describes how a returned flow spec could indicate the service offered, while noting that a changed specification could be only a hint.

The memo identifies limitations in its loss model, its single delay-sensitivity point and its proposed set of guarantee choices. It leaves flow setup and negotiation outside scope. Its security discussion says authentication of requests belongs in the design of a negotiation protocol, not in the flow-specification data structure.
sections.plainLanguage: The guarantee field says how firmly the host wants the network to meet the request. The memo calls the format an early proposal and identifies parts that may need improvement.
